topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: CBT, talking therapies and motivational interviewing
blurb: Explain the CBT model, place people on the stepped-care ladder and use OARS and the stages of change to support change.
question: Kofi, 38, has low mood (PHQ-9 score 11). He says, 'I messed up one report, so I'm useless at everything,' and he has stopped seeing friends. He also drinks heavily but says he 'might cut down one day'. How should the nurse help?

teach.h: CBT: how we think shapes how we feel
teach.body: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a structured, time-limited, collaborative talking therapy. It works on the links between thoughts, feelings, physical sensations and behaviour in the here and now, and uses homework between sessions. NICE describes it as goal-oriented and focused on current issues, teaching coping skills. Plain English: change the unhelpful thought or the unhelpful action, and the feeling usually follows.

teach.caption: Each part feeds the others. Avoidance stops the person testing the thought, so the cycle keeps going.

head: Thinking error
Example
rows: 'If it's not perfect, it's a failure'
'One mistake means I'm useless at everything'
teach.caption: CBT helps the person notice the thought, weigh the evidence and try a more balanced alternative.

teach.h: Stepped care for depression and anxiety
teach.caption: NG222: less severe depression (PHQ-9 under 16): least intrusive first, usually guided self-help; no routine antidepressant first line. CG113 uses 4 steps for GAD.

teach.h: NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and depression
teach.caption: NHS England: treats depression, GAD, panic, OCD, PTSD, social anxiety, health anxiety, phobias and more.
MI is a collaborative conversation that draws out the person's own reasons for change rather than persuading or confronting.
Match the approach to the stage: explore ambivalence in contemplation, help plan in preparation.

teach.body: Kofi's PHQ-9 of 11 places him in NG222's 'less severe' group, so the nurse offers the least intrusive option first, such as guided self-help, and tells him he can self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies. She names his overgeneralising gently and explains how avoiding friends keeps his mood low. On alcohol he is in contemplation, so she uses OARS: 'What would be different if you drank less?' and reflects his own reasons, without lecturing.

teach.text: Arguing or warning harder ('You must stop drinking now') usually increases resistance: MI rolls with ambivalence instead. And for less severe depression, antidepressants are NOT routinely first line (NG222); offer the least intrusive treatment, often guided self-help, unless the person prefers otherwise.

items: CBT links thoughts, feelings, body and behaviour; structured, time-limited, collaborative, with homework.
Thinking errors: all-or-nothing, overgeneralising, catastrophising, mind reading, should statements.
Stepped care: least intrusive first; NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) accepts self-referral.
MI uses OARS; stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance (relapse possible).

summary: You can now explain the CBT model, recognise thinking errors and place a person on the stepped-care ladder. You can also use OARS and the stages of change to support someone who is unsure about changing.

A.q: Which statement best describes cognitive behavioural therapy?
options: Open-ended exploration of childhood conflicts
Structured, time-limited work on thoughts and behaviour
Advice-giving sessions directed by the therapist
A single session reliving a traumatic event
A.why: CBT is structured, time-limited and collaborative, focusing on how current thoughts, feelings and behaviour interact, with homework between sessions.

whyNot.2: CBT is collaborative, not directive advice-giving.
whyNot.3: Single-session reliving is not CBT and is not recommended after trauma.

A.q: In motivational interviewing, what does the 'R' in OARS stand for?
options: Reassurance
Reframing
Reflections
Rewards
A.why: OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries.

whyNot.0: Reassurance can close down discussion and is not an OARS skill.
whyNot.1: Reframing is used in CBT and MI but is not the R in OARS.
whyNot.3: Rewards are not part of OARS.

A.q: A man says, 'I know my drinking is a problem, but I'm not ready to do anything yet.' Which stage of change is he in?
options: Contemplation
Precontemplation
Preparation
Action
A.why: Contemplation: aware of the problem and ambivalent, without a plan to change yet.

whyNot.1: In precontemplation the person does not see a problem.
whyNot.2: Preparation involves planning to change soon.

B.q: Sara, 26, with a PHQ-9 of 9, has a new episode of low mood and asks what NICE recommends first. What should the nurse explain?
options: An SSRI is the usual first-line treatment
Inpatient care is the safest first option
Group therapy is needed before any self-help
Guided self-help is usually tried first
B.why: NG222: for less severe depression (PHQ-9 under 16), consider the least intrusive treatment first, guided self-help; do not routinely offer antidepressants first line unless that is her preference.

whyNot.0: Antidepressants are not routinely first line for less severe depression.
whyNot.1: Inpatient care is far beyond what less severe depression needs.
whyNot.2: Guided self-help is the least intrusive option and need not wait for groups.

B.q: During CBT, Ana says, 'My friend didn't text back, so she must hate me.' Which thinking error is this?
options: Mind reading
Catastrophising about her health
Black-and-white thinking
Should statements
B.why: Mind reading: assuming you know what someone else thinks without evidence.

whyNot.1: Catastrophising imagines the worst outcome, such as a disaster.
whyNot.2: Black-and-white thinking sees things in extremes such as total success or failure.
whyNot.3: Should statements are rigid rules about how one must behave.

B.q: Using motivational interviewing, which response to a person who says 'Cannabis helps me relax' is most appropriate?
options: 'Cannabis will make your psychosis worse.'
'You need to stop before your next clinic appointment.'
'So it helps you relax. What are the downsides for you?'
'Why would you keep using it with your diagnosis?'
B.why: A reflection followed by an open question explores ambivalence and draws out the person's own reasons for change, the core of MI.

whyNot.0: Warning or confronting tends to increase resistance.
whyNot.1: Directing change ignores where he is and his own motivation.
whyNot.3: A 'why' question can sound judgemental and provoke defensiveness.

C.q: Mr Jones has generalised anxiety. Psychoeducation and guided self-help have not helped and his anxiety now affects work. Under NICE CG113 stepped care, what is offered next?
options: A further course of guided self-help
Long-term benzodiazepine treatment
Admission to a specialist inpatient unit
A choice of CBT, applied relaxation or a drug
C.why: CG113 step 3: inadequate response to step 2 or marked functional impairment: choice of high-intensity psychological intervention (CBT or applied relaxation) or drug treatment.

whyNot.0: Repeating step 2 ignores the inadequate response.
whyNot.1: Benzodiazepines are not offered except short-term in crisis.
whyNot.2: Inpatient care is step 4 for complex, refractory GAD with very marked impairment.

C.q: Kofi has agreed to cut down drinking and says, 'I've already bought alcohol-free beer and I'm starting Monday.' Which stage is he in and what helps most now?
options: Contemplation: explore pros and cons further
Preparation: help him make a concrete plan
Maintenance: focus on relapse prevention
Precontemplation: give information on risks
C.why: Preparation: intending to act soon and taking small steps; help him firm up a specific, realistic plan.

whyNot.0: He has moved past ambivalence to planning.
whyNot.2: Maintenance follows a sustained period of change.

C.q: After 3 weeks of CBT homework, Leah says she no longer avoids the supermarket but still thinks 'people are staring'. What is the most CBT-consistent next step?
options: Test the thought with a behavioural experiment
Stop CBT, as the thought has not changed
Tell her firmly that nobody is looking at her
Return to avoidance until the thought fades
C.why: CBT treats thoughts as testable ideas: a behavioural experiment gathers evidence for and against 'people are staring', building on her progress.

whyNot.1: Behaviour change is progress; thoughts often shift later.
whyNot.2: Simple reassurance is not collaborative evidence-gathering.
whyNot.3: Avoidance maintains anxiety in the CBT model.

reteach.title: Thoughts, actions, readiness
reteach.question: How do CBT and MI fit together?

blocks.body: MI builds readiness: it helps someone who is unsure find their own reasons to change. CBT gives the method once they are ready: spot thinking errors, test thoughts, change avoidance. Use MI's OARS when someone says 'maybe one day', and CBT skills when they say 'I want to change'.

explain.body: Thoughts, feelings, physical sensations and behaviour interact; changing thoughts or behaviour changes feelings. Structured, collaborative, homework.

test.q: In the CBT model, why does avoidance keep anxiety going?
options: It raises levels of stress hormones permanently
It stops the person testing their fearful thought
It causes depression, which then causes anxiety
It weakens the therapeutic relationship over time
test.why: Avoidance brings short-term relief but prevents the person discovering the feared outcome does not happen, so the belief and anxiety persist.

whyNot.0: This is not the CBT explanation.
whyNot.2: Avoidance maintains anxiety directly, not via depression.
whyNot.3: The CBT maintenance cycle concerns untested beliefs.

explain.body: Least intrusive first. Less severe depression: guided self-help; no routine antidepressant first. GAD: education and monitoring, then low intensity, then high intensity or drug, then specialist.

test.q: Which treatment does NICE NG222 suggest considering first for a new episode of less severe depression?
options: Electroconvulsive therapy
Individual psychodynamic therapy for 2 years
An antidepressant plus individual CBT
Guided self-help
test.why: NG222: all table 1 treatments can be first line, but consider the least intrusive and least resource-intensive first: guided self-help.

whyNot.0: ECT is for severe, life-threatening depression.
whyNot.1: This is neither least intrusive nor an NG222 first choice.
whyNot.2: Combination treatment is listed for more severe depression.

explain.body: Open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries: drawing out the person's own motivation.

test.q: Which statement is an affirmation in motivational interviewing?
options: 'Have you thought about stopping drinking this month?'
'You've cut down twice before; that took real effort.'
'So you're saying it feels hard to stop right now.'
'You should join a support group in your area soon.'
test.why: An affirmation recognises the person's strengths and efforts, building confidence to change.

whyNot.3: This is advice-giving, not an affirmation.

explain.body: Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance; relapse can happen at any point and is part of the cycle.

test.q: A woman says she does not see any problem with her daily gambling. Which stage of change is she in?
options: Contemplation
Preparation
Precontemplation
Maintenance
test.why: Precontemplation: the person is not yet considering change and may not see a problem.
